$comment: The M4 Part B card schema, as data. Two things read this file and nothing else defines the decks: scripts/validate-decks.mjs (Node, zero deps) and src/game/voice/cards.ts (the engine's loader). A writer tuning a deck changes the JSON here and both sides follow. 'required' tags must be present and in 'values'; optional tags may be absent, and 'default' says what the engine assumes when they are. 'coverage' lists the tag tuples the validator reports zero-card gaps for. 'alias' maps a legacy tag name onto its modern one, so the M3 files still validate.

burnTiers.run-to-run: Never repeated across runs: burned in localStorage until the deck is exhausted, then reshuffled.

$commonFieldsNote: M4b §A.2 and §A.5. Two fields every card in every deck may carry, written TOP-LEVEL — siblings of `tags`, not inside it. `motifs` is a list and `tags` is for the single values the dealer matches on; `weather` excludes a card from the night outright rather than ranking it, which is not what a tag does either. The engine also reads `tags.motifs` and `tags.weather`, so a deck written the other way still scores, and arrivals keeps its M4 `tags.weather` where its own spec requires it.

motifs.$note: One to three words from content/motifs.json and nowhere else. The validator rejects anything outside that vocabulary and reports per-deck coverage. Zero is allowed on a card with no image in it.

weather.$note: The sky the card implies, including by its clothing — a raincoat, a collar turned up, wet boots. A card that names another sky than the night's never appears in that run.

$commonTagsNote: M4b §A.3. One tag every deck may carry, merged underneath each deck's own, so a deck that already declares it — portraits.gender is required, business.gender has been optional since M4 — keeps its own stricter spec. It marks a card with a gendered pronoun in it; the engine filters on the subject's gender for similes about a body or a voice, and for business.
$vocabFilesNote: A vocabulary too long to keep in two places lives in its own file, and both readers — scripts/validate-decks.mjs and src/game/voice/cards.ts — resolve it from there. The motif vocabulary is the only one so far: 70 words in seven groups, and duplicating it here is how it would drift.

story.$comment: The closing story: what really happened, told by the detective after the verdict (src/game/story.ts). One card is one beat of the night in order, and every slot is filled from a truth field of the case: nothing a card says may be a fact the case does not hold, and no card names a secret, a lie, a noise branch or another suspect. A card's own words carry a fact only through its tags — `method` cards describe that method's weapon and wound (from the means and method templates), `anchor` cards that anchor's trace, `relationship` × `variant` cards one backstory template, `archetype` × `variant` cards one victim standing — and the story test checks each against the case. Plain words only: no genre jargon. {actor} is the culprit's surname and {actorFull} the full name ({he} {his} {him} {himself} theirs); {victim} and {victimFull} the victim ({vhe} {vhis} {vhim}); {scene} where it happened; {place} the place a beat is about; {time} and {until} spoken hours, {vtime} the victim’s arrival, {span} how long one waited for the other; {timing} the anchor's phrase and {anchorPlace} where it was; {aTaken}/{taken} the thing stolen; {goods} where it went; {where} where the missing person went; {found} where the body or the loss was found; {finder} who found it and {seer} who saw the missing person last; {year} {third} {tplace} {spouse} from the tie; {role} the culprit’s line of work and {vrole} the victim’s, {tie} the relationship; {weapon} the weapon, definite.

portrait-pairs.$note: Hone 1 Track C. A portrait written as a detail with the reason it is seen, in two or three plain sentences: "She kept her left hand in the pocket until she sat down. When she took it out I saw why: the little finger had been broken once and never set." The portraits deck holds a trait, a habit and a piece of clothing as three independent cards, and no assembly rule can make a card follow a detail it does not know the noun of. `recall` is the phrase a later page calls the person by — "the broken finger" — so the detail comes back rather than being replaced. `{He}` `{he}` `{his}` `{him}` are filled from the person's gender; write the capitalised form where the sentence starts on it. M8 §4: `recallAction` is the same detail as something the person does, past tense, for a later page of the night — "The coin was going over Kreuzer's knuckles again." — with `{name}` for the surname; a pair without one is never recalled on a night page, because a recall is never a noun.

business.$genderNote: A business card that says 'he' or 'she' belongs to a person of that gender and to nobody else — 'folded the newspaper she'd been reading' on a man is the tell. Tag every card that carries a gendered pronoun; a card with no pronoun in it is 'any' and goes to anybody. The engine treats this as a filter and not as a preference: it would rather deal a card of the wrong temper than one that calls a woman 'he'.

dashiell-lines.$slotNote: {name} is the SUBJECT of the question — whoever or whatever Dashiell is asking about — and never the person he is asking. The two coincide for exactly two kinds: 'ask-evening' and 'ask-hired' are questions about the person in front of him, so there {name} is the addressee. Everywhere else, use {addressee} for a vocative ('The {object}, {addressee}.') and {name} only for the subject ('Tell me about {name}.'). {place} and {object} are the place or thing the question is about, not the room the page happens in. A card with {name} is dealt only when the topic names a person; a topic that names none — an anchor, a noise — is asked for with {topic}.

utterances.$comment: The engine adds four slots to Part B's four, because four fact kinds carry something none of {subject}/{place}/{time}/{object} can hold: {window} (the coroner's span), {motive}, {method} and {secret}. An utterance that does not carry its fact kind's mandatory slots (see mandatorySlots) does not fit, and the engine falls back to the clue's flat text in quotation marks and logs the gap.

warnSlots.fact: the clue's own record has nowhere to land inside the card, so the engine appends it as a second sentence instead of the writer choosing where it falls

endings.$burnNote: A.8 names similes, portraits and asides as the run-to-run decks and does not name this one. The closing page is scored by a pure function that is recomputed on every render, so it has nowhere to write a burn; the card is drawn off the case seed instead, which keeps one case's ending the same however many times it is looked at.
endings.$m5Note: M5 §5. The endings are keyed by case type and by trope as well as by outcome. `caseType` defaults to `murder`, which is what the first thirty cards are; the sixteen robbery and disappearance cards name theirs, two to each (type, outcome) at par. Every cell the engine can reach now has a card, so the engine's hand-written closings are the body of the page and the deck is its last line, exactly as for a murder — the gap is logged only when the draw comes back empty. `coverage` stays on outcome × parDelta: extending it to the case types would report every unwritten trope cell as a gap on every run.

tags.$outcomeNote: `solved` was `hanged` until this deck had cards for a robbery and a disappearance. The axis names the outcome, not one case type's form of it: nobody goes to the gallows over a strongbox, and finding somebody alive is not a verdict. The cards that are about a hanging still say so in their own words.

office.$comment: M4b §B.2.1. Two rooms over a tailor's, at midnight, before anybody has knocked. This is the one deck where Dashiell's circumstance is allowed to be plot: behind on rent means the envelope is on the desk and the retainer matters. One card is the first paragraph of every run, so the deck is small and every card in it has to be able to open a book.

entrances.$comment: M4b §B.2.2. How the client comes through the door. The engine weaves the client's portrait into this per §A.4, so a card should leave room for a person rather than describe one: what the door did, what they did with their hat, how long they stood there. `familiar: yes` is for a client Dashiell already knows — the roll says so — and the card may say as much.

hiring.$comment: M4b §B.2.3. The exchange that hires him, as one frame. `{fact}` is the client's own clue — why Dashiell was hired — and `{retainer}` is what the money looks like on the desk, by the client's class: twenty dollars from a working man, fifty from a professional, a hundred from money, and a roll with a rubber band round it from the underworld. The engine fills `{retainer}`; a card that leaves it out gets no money in it, and this is the one page where the money is the point.
hiring.$pronounNote: Hone 3 §5. A hiring card is two or three sentences about one person, and seven of them named the client in both: "…," Kreuzer said. I took a roll before Kreuzer had gotten halfway through the second sentence. The second mention takes a pronoun, and the engine supplies the three cases for the client the card was dealt for — `{pronoun}` she/he, `{them}` her/him, `{their}` her/his — so the card stays one card rather than becoming two with a gender tag on each. Say the name first and the pronoun after, never the other way about.

warnSlots.retainer: the page never says what the job pays, and §B.2 asks that the player always knows they are being paid

witness.legacy: M3's one-card-per-answer deck. The M4 exchange is built from frames × dashiell-lines × utterances instead, so nothing deals this any more. Kept so the file still validates and so a writer can mine it.

errand.$comment: M6 §2. Why the detective came, first on every page that moved him. Derived from the notebook, never invented: `because` is what sent him (a person said it, a paper named it, a thing found somewhere pointed here), `for` is the lead's shape. {name} is the person who said it, {from} is the room the paper or the thing came out of, {who} is the person he came to ask, {subject} is what the errand is about, {place} is here. Plain register, one clause of figure at most. `searched` only matters for a no-lead return. `reachable` lists the tag pairs the engine can deal; the validator reports each one below `minPerCoverageCell`, and a test holds each of them to three cards. M8 §6: `bridged: yes` marks the short form, dealt when an earlier page’s bridge already named this lead and said why ("Kreuzer would know where the secretary had been").

hours.$comment: M6 §3. The clock's beats. `hour` when an action carries the clock across an hour ({hour} is the hour's word, one to seven), `two-left` when two calls remain, `last-call` when one does. Each replaces the page's passage-of-time beat and never adds to it.

establish.$comment: M8 §3. The first visit to a place: one paragraph saying what the place is and what kind of place it is, how you get in, what it is at this hour, and how the weather has emptied or filled it. Keyed by the place template id (src/gen/data/places.ts) plus `office`. {watcher} is the surname of the fixture posted there and {owner} the surname of whose place it is (the victim, for the victim’s address); either may be absent, and a card that names an absent slot is never dealt, so every place needs cards without them. The watch clause follows from the `watch` deck; the weather may be added by the engine.

watch.$comment: M8 §3. The clause in the establish paragraph that says who watches the place, keyed by the watcher’s fixture role, or `none` for an unwatched place ("nobody minds who uses the stairs"). {watcher} is the watcher’s surname and never appears on a `none` card.

return.$comment: M8 §3. One line for a return visit. `scene` is the room the night opened in (where the body, or the empty shelf, is); the rest are keyed by the place’s kind. {place} is the place’s short name, lower case ("the speakeasy"), and may open a sentence.

activity.$comment: M8 §4. What a person present is doing when the detective walks in: one sentence, from their trade, the place and the hour. Chosen once per visit and kept for it. `role` is the suspect archetype id or the fixture role (`any` is the engine’s own fallback). `band`: after-midnight is 12:00–2:59, small-hours 3:00–5:59, dawn 6:00–8:00; `any` fits all three. {name} is the surname and opens the card; never a pronoun for {name}, whose gender varies. {place} is the short name. `at: work` marks a trade task on a suspect card: dealt only where that archetype works (WORKPLACES in src/game/scene/plan.ts); anywhere else the person does what anybody does there. M9: `place`, a place template id, marks a card that only reads right in that one room (racking cues is the pool hall's, not the pawnshop's); it is dealt nowhere else.

thought.$comment: M8 §5. What the detective makes of it, one class a card. Slots, by class: clears/implicates/contradicts — {subject} the person placed, {place} where, {time} the spoken hour, {other} the scene (clears) or the place they claimed (contradicts); implicates with basis `access` has only {subject}. observer-placed — {source} the one who saw it, {subject} whom they saw, {place}, {time}. unmentioned — {source}, {place}, {time}; `via: office` when the client left it out of the briefing, `account` when a told evening omits it. motive — {subject}, {victim}. method — {other} the thing, {place}, {victim}. window — basis `anchor`: {other} the anchor as a noun ("the El going over"), {time}; basis `coroner`: no anchor. not-robbery — {victim}, {place}. robbery-shape and goods — {other} the thing taken, {place}. secret and dead-end — {subject}. context — {victim}. nothing — {place}. last-seen and seen-after (missing cases) — {victim}, {place}, {time}. view — the detective’s view of a person on arrival: {subject}, keyed by `who` (watcher, client, known, stranger) and `lied`. {scene} on any card is the short name of the room it happened in, {victim} the victim's surname, and {time} always the spoken hour ("ten o’clock", "half past nine"). A thought may say "if" and "would"; it never asserts a fact the notebook does not hold. Never a pronoun for a slotted person. touches (M9, bases and slots in $m9) — what one fact touches on the grid, a place and a half hour on somebody’s row, and never what it proves.
thought.$nightHone1: Night Hone 1: every card names at least one slot, because a thought that names nothing says nothing the reader did not have. New slots: {means} the method as a noun phrase ("poison in a drink") and {how} what whoever did it had to do first ("had to get at the chloral and doctor the drink"), on method; {motive} the subject's motive told afterwards ("stood to inherit from Sweeney"), on motive; {span} the coroner's hours said aloud ("from half past nine until eleven"), on window with basis `coroner`. {other} on secret and dead-end is what the secret was, as something a person had been doing ("selling stolen goods"). New classes: `absent` — {subject} was not at {place} at {time}; `hint` — somebody noticed {subject} hiding something. New bases: window `dead-by` / `alive-at` — {victim} dead by, or alive at, {time}; context `self` and `account` — {subject} told me who they are, or their evening; context `outside` — {subject} at {place} at {time}, outside the hours that matter; contradicts `at` (placed at {place}, claimed {other}) and `not-at` (claimed {place}, said not to be there). nothing — {place} on a search, {subject} on a question.
thought.$m9: M9 (docs/20-m9-deduction.md §2). New class `touches`: what one fact touches on the grid (who was where, by the half hour), never what it proves. Ids tht-m###. Bases and slots: `placement` — {subject} at {place} at {time}, inside the hours that matter, not {scene}; `described` — {source} saw a stranger, {other} the description ("a man in his thirties"), at {place} at {time}; `absence` — {source}, who works at {place}, says nobody came in at {time} but those named; `count` — {source} counted {other} ("two people") at {place} at {time}; `anchored` — {subject} at {place} when {other} (an event as a noun phrase, "the El going over"), clock hour not known yet; `timing` — {other} happened at {time}; `account` — {subject}’s own evening in {subject}’s own words, the one kind of statement that can be false, and the card never says whether it is; `stranger` — {source} did not know {subject}, or said so; `together` — {subject} and {name} in the same place at {time}; `apart` — {subject} and {name} never in the same place all evening; `said` — after a confrontation, {subject}’s new words put {subject} at {place} at {time}. {scene} and {victim} are allowed on any; `case: murder` on a card that speaks of a death or the killing.

bridge.$comment: M8 §6. The next lead, named, and why. `tie: victim` — {subject} is a person and {tie} their relation to the victim ("Sweeney’s secretary"). `tie: place` — {subject} is a person who keeps a place and {tie} says so ("the landlady at the third floor"). `tie: time` — {tie} is the spoken hour the notebook’s window opens on ("half past nine") and {subject} whom or what the question is about: the victim, a person, or a topic ("the noise", "the lock"). {who} is the person to ask and {where} where they are found (absent when the notebook does not know). `lead: search` (a card with no {who}) is the bridge to a room to go through, {subject} its short name; every other card is `lead: ask`, the default.

carry.$comment: M8 §2. The reason for a search or a question at the same place, one sentence, first on the page. `lead: yes` when an open lead points at it, `no` for an unmarked choice ("No one sent me to it"). {who} is the person asked, {subject} what about (the thing searched, for search-thing), {name} the person whose word sent me, absent when a paper or a room did. Cards must read with {name} absent.

answer.$comment: M8 §2. What came of the errand, when no thought already says it. `found`: what I came for; `dead-end`: not, and the lead was a dead end; `something-else`: not, but something else. {subject} is what the errand was about and {name} who sent me; either may be absent.

place-ambient.$comment: Night Hone 1. What a place is like to stand in: its sounds, its light, its smells, what is on its walls, in one or two past-tense sentences. Dealt on a search after the finds and on a return visit. Keyed by place template id and hour band (after-midnight 12:00–2:59, small-hours 3:00–5:59, dawn 6:00–8:00, or any). No people (nor that the place is empty or full), no weather, no clock, no anchor, nothing that matters to a case, no figures.

search-act.$comment: Night Hone 1. How the detective goes through a place, in its own terms: the path and the surfaces looked at, two or three sentences, first person, past tense. Never what was or was not there — the finds follow in the same paragraph. Keyed by place template id.

crowd.$comment: Night Hone 1. People in a room the case has given the detective no reason to single out yet, said together in one sentence. {group} opens the card: a plural noun phrase the engine builds ("Two men and a woman", "Lanza and a man I didn't know"), two to five people, the verb after it plural. They are only ever they/them. Keyed by place template id and hour band.

decide.$comment: Night Hone 1. The decision after a catch (golden page 5: "I didn't ask her about it. Not yet. A client who leaves things out is still a client, and she was paying."): what the detective does now about somebody a thought just caught — seen somewhere they never mentioned, or contradicted. `who`: client, watcher or suspect. `act`: hold (not yet), press (put it to them), note (mark it and come back); derived from who it is and their temper. `present`: yes when they are in the room. {subject} their surname, {place} and {time} where and when they were caught; {they}/{them}/{their} their pronouns, filled by the engine.

confront.$comment: M9 §3. Putting a fact to somebody ("Put it to Hanrahan."): the detective reads a person a fact from the notebook that crosses what they said about themselves. `outcome`: wrong — the fact touches nothing they told me; second-lie — a new story for the same hours; quiet — they stop talking about it (the engine prints "{subject} has nothing more to say about it."); admit — they give up where they were and what they were keeping back; hold — they keep to what they said; withdraw — somebody who said they were with another person takes it back. `part`: reaction — right after the fact is read and right before their words, what they did on hearing it (a pause, a look, something put down), never what they answer and never a judgement of it; on `wrong` the reaction carries their words, exactly “That doesn’t touch anything I told you.”; close — after their words, one or two sentences on what the detective did with it (wrote it down, looked at the grid, left it), never a verdict. {subject} their surname, on every card; {they}/{them}/{their} their pronouns, filled lower case by the engine, so never first in a sentence; {place} the place the fact is about and {time} its spoken hour, either may be absent, so each is on a minority of cards.
